title: Studio Ghibli adds new Princess Mononoke sukajan jacket to its anime streetwear range in Japan
description: Ghibli shines a spotlight on Japanese street fashion with this stylish new release. Studio Ghibli has long been a champion of Japanese culture, both in its movie storylines and its merchandise ranges. Right now, that support for Japan and its culture is clearly evident in a new release from the studio’s GBL brand, which specialises […]
content:
Ghibli shines a spotlight on Japanese street fashion with this stylish new release.

Studio Ghibli has long been a champion of Japanese culture, both in its movie storylines and its merchandise ranges. Right now, that support for Japan and its culture is clearly evident in a new release from the studio’s GBL brand, which specialises in cool streetwear influenced by American fashion, and it’s called the Princess Mononoke Velveteen Sukajan jacket.

As the name suggests, this new product celebrates the studio’s 1997 animated feature film Princess Mononoke, with a design that includes a cute nod to the year of the movie’s release.

▼ A kodama forest spirit sits in place of the second “9” in 1997.

The sukajan is a Japanese souvenir jacket, traditionally decorated with elaborate embroidery depicting motifs like Japanese landscapes, animals and mythical creatures. The style became popular among American servicemen stationed in Japan after World War II, specifically in the area of Yokosuka in Tokyo’s neighbouring Kanagawa Prefecture, who commissioned embroidered jackets as souvenirs. Today, sukajan represent a unique facet of Japanese streetwear, making it a perfect item for the American-influenced GBL brand.

This particular sukajan is an updated version of a jacket originally released in 2019. This new design features a large image of heroine San riding giant wolf Moro on the back…

▼ … and images of the boar god Okkoto (known as “Okkoto-nushi” in Japanese) embroidered on the front.

▼ The deep moss-green colour is inspired by the forests in the film.

The jacket has a convenient inner pocket, and the bright terracotta lining contrasts nicely with the vivid green, creating a stylish flash of colour when the jacket is unzipped.

Another unique feature is the fabric – unlike the shiny satin frequently associated with sukajan, this version is made from velveteen, which gives it a softer look, with just a hint of sheen.

▼ It also has insulating padding, making it suitable for colder weather, and a beautiful tag featuring deer god Shishigami.

Other details include a ribbed collar, cuffs and hem, a YKK zipper and slash pockets on the front. The embroidery is made using a dimensional hand-guided technique, giving the designs a raised, textured appearance.

The jacket is available in four unisex sizes, from S to XL, and the model in these photos is 173 centimetres (5 feet 8 inches) tall and wears a size XL.

Sukajan are generally made to last and are priced as such, with this one retailing for 39,600 yen (US$248). While the jacket was made available online from 14 November, it’s set to be stocked at GBL retail stores in Japan from 21 November.

title: Tokyo’s Shibuya Sakurazaka cherry blossom street to be decommissioned, number of trees to increase
description: Shibuya’s cherry blossom hill to live on and become pinker than ever. content:
Shibuya’s cherry blossom hill to live on and become pinker than ever.

Usually, when people think of Tokyo’s Shibuya neighborhood, they think of the famous Shibuya Scramble intersection and statue of faithful dog Hachiko, plus trendy fashion shops, lively bars, and tourist-friendly pop culture specialty stores. All of those things are indeed iconic parts of Shibuya, but they’re all located on the northwest side of Shibuya Station.

Meanwhile, if you head just a block or two southwest from the station, you’ll find something you might not expect in a part of the city known for urban exuberance: an ascending street lined with beautiful cherry blossom trees.

▼ It’s actually a really pretty place even when the sakura aren’t in bloom.

The road is called Sakurazaka, meaning “cherry blossom hill,” a much more poetic moniker than its other name, Ward Road 1032. That designation is important, though, as the Shibuya Ward government has announced that it will be decommissioning Sakurazaka as part of the ongoing property development construction that’s been taking place in the district.

The disparity in economic activity between the area to the northwest of Shibuya Station and those on its other sides hasn’t escaped the notice of real estate investors. In recent years, a number of new commercial and office high-rises developments have gone up, such as the Hikarie, Shibuya Scramble Square, and Shibuya Stream buildings to the east and southeast of the station. Now developers are turning their attention in earnest to the area to the southwest of the station, for a development to be called “Next Shibuya Sakurazaka.”

▼ Shibuya Station (渋谷駅) and the site of Next Shibuya Sakurazaka (marked in pink)

The development will be subdivided into three sections, currently called Blocks A, B, and C. Block A is planned to be a 35-floor skyscraper with offices, shops, a concert hall with a capacity of 2,000 attendees, and a bus terminal.

However, Block A is going to be built, map-wise, right on top of Sakurazaka. Marked in blue on the map below are Sakurazaka (Ward Road 1032) and two perpendicular ward-administered roads within the current street network…

…and here are the sites that Blocks A, B, and C are going to be built on.

“Downtown Tokyo loses cherry blossom road in order to build shops and offices” would be a story that would induce tears, anger, or some combined result of moist rage among many people, but there is a silver lining to all this. Yes, Sakurazaka is going to be decommissioned as a ward-administered road, and the property developers do plan to build over the existing road’s asphalt. What they’re not planning to do, though, is get rid of the cherry blossom trees.

Instead, as shown in the preview image above, the existing sakura are being incorporated into the new development’s design, in what appears will be a walkable, publicly accessible part of the center. What’s more, the plan is to actually increase the number of cherry blossom tress. The street currently has 29 trees, but the developers want Block A to have 40 to 50, largely expanding the amount of sakura to be seen.

It’s not clear if each and every tree on Sakurazaka will be retained in its current position, as some may need to be removed for safety reasons based on their age. Nevertheless, it’s clear that the developers aren’t looking to just chop them all down and pour dull gray concrete all across the hill.

The decommissioning of Ward Road 1032 isn’t going to be a great loss for transportation infrastructure either. Originally, the road was supposed to stretch to Jiyu-dori Street in Meguro Ward’s Higashigaoka neighborhood, but instead it tapers and dissolves long before reaching that point. That initial plan was created not long after the end of World War II, and in the ensuing years that it’s been stalled several other roads that serve that purpose have been built, leading the Shibuya Ward administration to deem it unnecessary in its most recent once-a-decade reevaluation.

▼ Shibuya Sakurazaka at night this past spring

All things considered, it’s probably not such a bad turn of events for Shibuya’s Sakurazaka, and being an attractive feature of a commercial center gives the developers incentive to make sure the trees are properly cared for. That said, the atmosphere is probably going to be different than the more organic community vibe Sakurazaka has right now, so thankfully construction isn’t scheduled to start until 2030, meaning you’ve still got a few sakura season chances to see it as it is.

title: Foreign tourist missing after off-season Mt. Fuji hike, father reportedly offering reward to find him/his body
description: Two of three friends made the right decision to call off their Mt. Fuji hiking plans. In the first week of this month, a Chinese tourist in his 20s arrived in Japan with two friends. The trio then made their way to Yamamanshi, drawn to the prefecture, like many others, by Mt. Fuji, which straddles […]
content:
Two of three friends made the right decision to call off their Mt. Fuji hiking plans.

In the first week of this month, a Chinese tourist in his 20s arrived in Japan with two friends. The trio then made their way to Yamamanshi, drawn to the prefecture, like many others, by Mt. Fuji, which straddles Yamanashi’s border with Shizuoka Prefecture.

The three didn’t go to Mt. Fuji to appreciate the sight of it from afar, though, but with the intention to climb Japan’s tallest mountain. However, Mt. Fuji’s climbing season has been finished for the year since early September, which is something the man’s friends weren’t aware of until after they got to Yamanashi.

That’s honestly kind of shocking. Despite how enticingly gentle its slopes may look from a distance, summiting Mt. Fuji is a strenuous endeavor, and one that can be very dangerous in the off-season, when the weather is colder, daylight hours shorter, and support facilities such as mountain huts aren’t operating. In recent years there have been an increasing number of rescue missions that had to be carried out in order to save off-season hikers, and pretty much any reputable website with Mt. Fuji climbing information will start with information on when the climbing season begins and ends.

As surprising as the gap in knowledge may have been, the man’s friends at least showed good wisdom by then deciding to call off their hike. The man himself, though, was now determined to go it alone. On the morning of November 8, he set off from the fifth station of Mt. Fuji’s Yoshida Trail, where regular road access ends. He was apparently in good spirits, sending text messages and videos to his friends who’d declined to make the climb with him.

Unfortunately, that was the last time anyone has heard from him. As of November 17, the man hasn’t returned or contacted any of his friends or family. According to one of the friends who came with him to Japan, he wasn’t equipped with any specialized winter hiking gear such as crampons for extra traction while walking potentially icy sections of the trail. He didn’t have a tent either, which is especially concerning since, what with it being the off-season, there are no mountain huts or other shelters that are currently staffed and operating on the mountain.

▼ “It is regrettable that someone would make the decision to recklessly climb [Mt. Fuji] while the mountain is closed to hikers,” said Fujiyoshida mayor Shigeru Horiuchi while discussing the situation.

Police are continuing to search for the missing man, but have found no sign of him yet. On November 13, five days after he went missing, the man’s father arrived in Japan. According to Chinese media reports, he has offered a reward of 500,000 yuan (approximately US$75,000) to anyone who can find his son while he’s still alive, and 100,000 should anyone discover his body.

The whole thing isn’t going over well with online commenters in Japan, whose reactions have included:

“First pay for the cost of the search and rescue operation.”
“If you’ve got many to toss around, give it straight to the rescue workers who’re looking for your son.”
“How does a guy like that even manage to make any friends in the first place?”
“Just leave him up there. Doesn’t matter what country you’re from. If you try to climb the mountain during the off-season, whatever happens is on you.”
“I hope this doesn’t end up making other people run off to Mt. Fuji to look for him and then end up needing to be rescued themselves.”

As for that last point, once again it should be stressed that hiking Mt. Fuji can be incredibly dangerous right now, so going to look for the son yourself really isn’t a bright idea, and that’s even without getting into the question of whether or not the Japanese authorities would even allow someone to accept/keep a reward earned through doing something you’re not supposed to (hiking Mt. Fuji at this time of year).

Hopefully the son can still be found and returned home safely, but for now this a solemn reminder to stay off of Mt. Fuji in the off-season.

title: Join Suica’s penguin on its graduation trip to outer space at Hotel Metropolitan Tokyo Ikebukuro

content:
Book a limited-time room with the beloved penguin mascot complete with free goodies, special foods, and a lottery to win a very large penguin figure.

With JR East planning to “graduate” the penguin mascot of its rechargeable Suica ID card early next year, fans are beginning to get nostalgic for all things related to the wing-waving little friend. For many, it feels like a bittersweet farewell knowing that the penguin who accompanied them to school and work every day for dozens of years will no longer grace the front of new Suica cards.

▼ This little guy’s been with me since 2010–and shockingly, I haven’t lost him once since then.

©SoraNews24

Luckily, Hotel Metropolitan Tokyo Ikebukuro of JR East Hotels has unveiled a new concept room that will appeal to anyone wishing to celebrate the penguin’s departure in high style. From December 22, 2026 through March 30, 2027, visitors can book a themed city-view room with a king-sized bed on the 22nd floor in which the penguin is taking its graduation trip to outer space. Only one room (maximum two people) is available per day, with check-in at 3 p.m. and check-out at 12 p.m. the following day.

The room will come with not only out-of-this-world decorations but also original goods, including two sets of this multi-ring strap set that can be used as a shoulder strap for a smartphone case and is customizable with space-themed Suica penguin charms.

Each guest will also receive a voucher to exchange for an adorable Suica Penguin Cake made from mascarpone and strawberry jelly. Just look at that little red bowtie!

▼ Suica Penguin Pancakes are another option for breakfast room service.

Furthermore, guests can try their hand at a special capsule lottery, limited to one try per room, to win collaborative, not-for-sale items such as pouches, mug cups, acrylic stands, t-shirts, and even marzipan.

For the final 15 days of the concept room beginning on March 16, the lottery will go all out with the addition of a special 95-centimeter (37.4-inch) penguin decoration, stand panels, plushies, bed runners, and tapestries for winning. Never fear if you’re coming from a distance because the hotel can ship any large items you score directly to your residence in Japan.

Finally, a limited-time room service option will include a Suica Penguin Roast Beef and Camembert Cheeseburger for 3,000 yen (US$18.79).

Hotel Metropolitan Tokyo Ikebukuro will begin taking reservations for the Suica penguin concept room on December 1 at 12 p.m. JST for dates of stay between December 22 and January 31 and on January 1 at 12 p.m. JST for dates of stay between February 1 and March 30. Rates are 47,800-62,100 yen for stays between December 22 and March 15 and 75,700 yen for stays between March 16 and March 30.

For what it’s worth, I will always stand by the Suica penguin and not its new successor, thank you very much.

title: Japan’s JR East reveals new train company mascot character, online comments aren’t kind
description: Filling the Suica Penguin’s shoes isn’t going to be easy. JR East/East Japan Railway Company hit a home run when it picked the original mascot for its Suica prepaid card system. Introduced at the same time as the system itself in 2001, the Suica Penguin was an instant success, giving a cute, approachable persona to […]
content:
Filling the Suica Penguin’s shoes isn’t going to be easy.

JR East/East Japan Railway Company hit a home run when it picked the original mascot for its Suica prepaid card system. Introduced at the same time as the system itself in 2001, the Suica Penguin was an instant success, giving a cute, approachable persona to what was at the time a novel way to pay for train fare and shopping purchases. In the two and a half decades since, the popularity of both Suica and its mascot have grown and grown, so it was a shock to many when, one year ago, JR East said it would be replacing the penguin with a new mascot.

▼ So long, Suica Penguin

With the Suica system having become deeply integrated in so many people’s daily lives, the changeover is a big deal. JR East started by having a selection committee sift through artist proposals, then picking out three finalists which were revealed in September, with the winner to be decided through online voting. The candidates were a squirrel…

…a rabbit…

…and some kind of large-eared creature with a mole-like companion riding in its satchel.

Polling ran from September 8 to September 23. JR East has now released the results, and the new Suica mascot is…

…the rabbit…-ish-looking thing.

This doesn’t appear to have been a narrow win, either. Out of a total 1,664,399 votes, 860,152 were for the rabbit. That’s 51.6 percent of the total, so unless one of the losing candidates got hardly any votes at all, the rabbit won by a substantial margin.

This doesn’t mean, though, that everyone is emotionally onboard with the rail company’s new mascot. Reactions to the announcement tweet from JR East have been almost entirely negative, with many calling the character, with its vacant, expressionless eyes and seemingly pasted-on smile, far more creepy than cute. The purple color is also an issue for many, seeing as how it’s an attention-grabbing hue with no connection to JR East’s standard color designs (the company’s image color is green), and to many it looks like the character is suffering from poisoned status in an RPG video game.

“That rabbit is seriously poisoned.”
“Poison Bunny.”
“Has me thinking of the Grimace Shake.”
“Lo, I can feel only darkness within it.”
“Man, they’re really going with the purple one…”
“Was hoping for anything but this.”
“This isn’t cute, and I can’t really tell what it’s supposed to be.”
“I love it. For real. It’s cute.”
“The penguin was cuter.”
“It’s got a Teletubby kind of thing going on, and it’s freaking me out. Should have stuck with the penguin.”
“Looks like some sort of monster from a horror video game.”
“Yep, definitely gonna be some crying kids [when they see the character] at the station.”

／
Suicaの新たなイメージキャラクターが決定しました
～お客さまから愛称を募集します～
＼

2026年9月、Suicaの新たなイメージキャラクターのデザイン候補3案を発表し、お客さま投票を実施した結果、総得票数1,664,399票のうち860,152票を獲得したのキャラクターに決定しました… pic.twitter.com/LX5RMveCHE

— JR 東日本ニュースリリース【公式】 (@JREast_News) November 18, 2026

The discrepancy between the rabbit being the clear favorite in voting but hardly anyone seeming to have anything to say about the design is surprising. One commenter wondered if the apparent landslide victory was a result of votes from those earnestly wanting a more conventionally cute character being split between the other options, while everyone wanting something weird or casting their vote as a joke then latched onto the rabbit with the unsettling expression. It’s also possible that the somewhat unfinished look of the squirrel (which lacks a visible outline) and the vagueness of the mole-and-friend design prevented them from really resonating with people wanting a conventionally cute mascot.

Of course, there is precedent for a mascot who’s initially seen as creepy-looking to win over the public. When the Osaka Expo 2025 made its mascot a lump of irregularly shaped tissue and eyeballs, more than a few people were shocked, but Myaku-Myaku has gone on to build a fanbase, even after the event’s finish. A major shift in public opinion came after Myaku-Myaku’s voice, and association personality, was added, and there’s a possibility for the new Suica mascot to follow the same playbook. JR East is currently accepting suggestions for the new character’s name through its website here, and the form also includes sections for submitters to write what kind of personality they want the rabbit to have.

Suggestions are being taken between now and December 15. Unlike with the mascot design, though, there will be no public voting this time, and instead the name will be selected by JR East. That’s probably for the best, since as of right now the most common suggestions online seem to be Bian (Japanese for “Option B,” as the rabbit was designated at its initial reveal), and Doku Usagi, which, as you can probably guess, means “Poison Bunny.”

title: Starbucks Japan reveals new Christmas advent calendar and holiday drinkware collection
description: Cosy new range covers everything from tumblers to bear blankets. Starbucks knows how to get into the holiday spirit in Japan, with festive Frappuccinos and a series of beautiful drinkware collections. Now, after treating us to a winter drinkware range and a Christmas-themed collection, the chain has just revealed it will be bringing out another […]
content:
Cosy new range covers everything from tumblers to bear blankets.

Starbucks knows how to get into the holiday spirit in Japan, with festive Frappuccinos and a series of beautiful drinkware collections. Now, after treating us to a winter drinkware range and a Christmas-themed collection, the chain has just revealed it will be bringing out another new range for the festive season, dubbed “Cosy Winter Moment“.

Featuring check patterns and snowflake motifs, this collection of limited-edition merchandise is designed to deliver warm and cosy vibes this winter, and it covers a wide range of goods, from tumblers, bottles and mugs right through to a bag, blanket, and even a never-before-seen advent calendar.

▼ Check Stainless Steel To-Go Bottle (5,750 yen)

This Starbucks-style cup-shaped stainless steel bottle features a locking lid, which unlocks by sliding the button across and pressing it down.

The gold-coloured base and check design gives the bottle a stylish look, complete with Bearista-shaped customisation boxes laser-etched onto the back.

The double-walled vacuum-insulated stainless steel construction provides excellent heat and cold retention, and the large, 473-millilitre (16-ounce) capacity will keep your thirst levels in check all day long.

▼ Cold Cup Tumbler with Ribbon – 710 millilitres (3,500 yen)

This tumbler features a Nordic-style design, with the navy colour offset by silvery snowflake motifs and a striking red lid with ribbon-adorned straw.

The ribbon accessory on the straw is detachable, and the knitted-like design on the cup gives it a cosy, wintery feel.

▼ Bear Shaped Check Mug – 355 millilitres (3,050 yen)

▼ This mug might look ordinary from the side…

▼ …but when viewed from above, you’ll see that it’s shaped like the face of a bear.

▼ The check design and cream interior give the beary cute mug a sophisticated look.

▼ Ribbon Heat-Resistant Glass Mug with Medal – 355 millilitres (3,400 yen)

▼ This blue-handled glass features a little bow near the base as a stylish accent…

▼ … and a medal-like siren logo for an added touch of shimmer and elegance.

▼ Ribbon Reusable Cup – 473 millilitres (500 yen)

▼ This cup features stars and red ribbons across a pale green background for fun festive appeal.

▼ Ribbon Reusable Cup + Ribbon Bearista Drink Hole Cap (1,150 yen)

If you’re willing to pay a bit more, you can splurge on this set, which includes the reusable cup and a figurine cap featuring the chain’s Bearista mascot, decked out with a ribbon and Santa hat.

▼ Simply insert the cap into the cup’s drink hole to prevent leaks and give it a playful look.

▼ Bottle Shoulder Bag (3,150 yen)

▼ If you’re looking for a stylish way to carry your bottle or tumbler around, this beautiful bag fits the bill.

Featuring a gorgeous navy blue hue, the bag includes a check drawstring lining, along with gold hardware for a touch of sparkle.

▼ The size has been carefully considered to ensure it fits the biggest bottle in the collection.

▼ Check Bearista Keychain (2,550 yen)

This warm and fluffy Bearista matches the collection in a check dress, and comes with a faux leather Starbucks charm and chain attachment.

▼ Snowflake Coaster (2,000 yen)

Sparkling snowflakes and delicate shimmer add a touch of elegance to this coaster, which is a perfect fit for the glass mug.

▼ Advent Calendar (11,000 yen)

▼ This advent calendar lets you count down to Christmas with a series of Starbucks products.

Unlike most advent calendars, which count down every day to Christmas, this set amps up the delayed gratification by spreading seven items out over 24 days.

You’ll be able to open a beautiful box every three to four days in December, and Starbucks hasn’t revealed what’s inside each box so it can be a surprise for customers.

▼ Pouch Set (2,600 yen)

▼ This set includes two pouches of different sizes, both made from a cosy material that’s warm to touch.

▼ The smaller bear-shaped pouch is ideal for storing small items like lipsticks.

▼ The pouches can be connected together with the included attachments, or detached and used separately.

▼ Gift Boxed Placemat Set (3,300 yen)

▼ This set of two check placemats will help bring the holiday collection together on your table.

Alternatively, the small 40 x 25 centimetre (16 x 10 inch) mats can be used at any time of the year to create a cosy cafe-at-home setting.

The bands, each of which comes with a Bearista-shaped gold metal charm, are a cute and convenient way to roll the mats up for storage.

▼ Packable Blanket (2,750 yen)

▼ This beautiful check blanket can be used as a lap blanket, or draped over your shoulders like a poncho.

▼ You can also pull the hood up, so you can cosplay as a bear while staying warm and cosy.

The back of the hood features a bear-shaped customisable box design, recalling the check-boxes seen on the back of Starbucks cups.

▼ The blanket can be folded and stored in the hood, so you can use it as a bear-eared cushion.

▼ Mini Pouch Gift with drink ticket (1,500 yen)

▼ This set includes a drink ticket…

▼ …and a cup-shaped pouch.

▼ The glittery fabric, with faux leather applique and champagne gold metal parts, gives the pouch a sophisticated look.

▼ It comes with a carabiner, so you can attach it to your bag and carry it around.

▼ The perfect size for holding lipstick, cards, and other small items.

▼ Mini Cup Gift Set with drink ticket (1,150 yen)

▼ This gift pack comes with a drink ticket and a sleeve on which you can write a message to the lucky recipient.

▼ The mini cup features the same check pattern as the larger goods in the collection.

While the cup is gorgeous on its own, the gift bag, with its wintery boa material and navy drawstring design, adds even more cosy appeal.

▼ The mini cup is gorgeous to look at, and practical too, as it be used to hold small trinkets and stationery.

▼ Beverage Card with drink ticket (750 yen)

Rounding out the collection is a wintry message card, adorned in the same check design as the wider collection.

The card includes a cute drink voucher, for one drink up to 687 yen for takeout or 700 yen for dine-in, valid until 27 May.

There’s a lot of winter cheer in this new collection, and as the products are only being made in limited numbers we’ll need to get in quick to avoid missing out on our favourites. The collection will be available online from 8 p.m. on 19 November, with in-store sales (excluding the online-limited products) commencing the next day, on 20 November. Happy holidays!

content:
Revenge is a dish best served fried with just the right seasoning.

While AI is increasingly becoming a part of society, there’s still a lot of confusion about exactly how it fits into our lives. Making ugly restaurant menus is all well and good, but how can we really harness its potential to make the future a better place to live?

This is a question one of SoraNews24’s greatest minds, Go Hatori, has long wrestled with and finally has an answer for. Long-time readers may recall that Go frequently tangles with online scammers of all types. He fearlessly engages with them and turns the tables by earning their trust instead, only to deprive them of their precious time on this planet with banal conversation that goes nowhere. Thus, the scammer becomes the scammed.

It’s not just something he does for funny articles either. Go has seriously established himself as a leading authority on online fraud in Japan, having written books, provided his expertise on TV, and given numerous lectures on the topic of online safety. Although there are lots of laughs along the way, his dedication to this pressing social issue is certainly no joke.

Now, armed with artificial intelligence, Go is planning a counteroffensive against con artists unlike any ever seen. He has converted his apartment into the First Recipe Division of the Fried Rice Unit (FRU), a non-governmental agency devoted to seeking out all online grifters, befriending them, and then stealing their fried rice recipes once their guard has been lowered.

How does he do this? Well, FRU is powered by a state-of-the-art-circa-2020 M1 Mac mini that he bought secondhand along with some wireless peripherals.

Due to the nature of its covert activities, FRU needs to operate in a completely separate environment from Go’s daily activities. The Mac mini does this on its own with Muse and ChatGPT agents. Go has set them up to lure in scammers via Instagram DMs into a dedicated account on the Japanese texting app Line. From there, the AIs engage in pleasant conversations with the crooks, all the while gently nudging the conversation towards fried rice.

Once a scammer is on the hook, the AIs alert Go, who takes over personally and secures the recipe. The main work is all done automatically, so he never bothered to get a monitor for the Mac mini, but he hooked it up to a projector for the occasional times when his personal input and maintenance are required. It has the added effect of looking really cool, which is a must for any counter-intelligence agency.

As Go stood back and gazed at his new FRU setup, he felt a slight pang. In doing this, he had become the thing he had sworn to fight. He had become the boss of a scamming ring.

Still, every conversation his FRU agents Chloe (Muse) and Nancy (ChatGPT) tie up a con artist with is one less conversation had with a potential victim. Getting a fried rice recipe from them in the process is just the icing on the cake.

But more than that, Go found through his own dealings with these people that getting them to offer up a fried rice recipe was a rare glimpse into the real person behind the lies. Perhaps in doing so, it reminds them of what it means to be human and to have compassion for others. But even if it doesn’t, Go can still try some new dishes.

▼ The FRU Central Mainframe also blends in seamlessly with Go’s decor.

So, swindlers and cheats of the world, you have been warned. The FRU is out there and, thanks to the relentless determination only a machine can provide, it will not stop until it has robbed all of you of your fried rice recipes. In fact, as of this writing, Go has already stolen one and will share it in an upcoming fraud food review!

title: FamilyMart’s “physical AI” robot workers getting chilly reception in Japan
description: Sure, it doesn’t do much, but it’s a robot! Even as AI is still in its early stages, many eager start-ups are looking at the next big thing, which they have dubbed “physical AI.” That really just means robots controlled by AI, but it seems to be a buzzword that piggybacks on the name recognition […]
content:
Sure, it doesn’t do much, but it’s a robot!

Even as AI is still in its early stages, many eager start-ups are looking at the next big thing, which they have dubbed “physical AI.” That really just means robots controlled by AI, but it seems to be a buzzword that piggybacks on the name recognition of “AI” itself.

In Japan, one company that has made great strides in actually putting physical AI to the test in real-world applications is Telexistence. Over the past few years, they have been developing robots to alleviate the labor shortages many convenience stores have been facing.

After a fair bit of testing, major convenience store chain FamilyMart announced that, starting next year, they would begin rolling out physical AI drink stockers to every location in Japan. These are AI-powered mechanical claws that are installed behind the drink section and constantly refill cans and bottles.

コンビニ大手のファミリーマートは、飲料を自動で補充するフィジカルAIを活用したロボットを本格導入する方針です。どんなロボットなのでしょうか。https://t.co/LvhlAmeiUY#nhk_video pic.twitter.com/iNwK0u3i5u

— NHKニュース (@nhk_news) November 12, 2026

Watching this system in action, two things are certain to spring to mind. First, it’s quite slow, but realistically, that should be fine since, unlike a human who would pop in and fill everything at once in a couple of minutes, this thing is working nonstop, around the clock. As long as it outpaces the rate people are buying drinks, it should be fine.

The more problematic observation is that the robot is moving drinks from a shelf to the fridge, which begs the question of how that first shelf was stocked. If a human is required to fill the shelf used by the robot to move the drinks into the fridge, then why not get the human to just stock the fridge directly?

According to FamilyMart, adoption of this system will reduce a human’s beverage stocking time by 70 percent. However, since beverage stocking is just one part of an employee’s many duties, it’s unclear how much real-world work that would equate to. Many readers of the news online were unconvinced it would amount to much in comments. People from both inside the industry and out came forward in saying they felt these machines have failed to impress.

“The shelves are restocked by robots from shelves restocked by humans. That’s called doing the same work twice.”
“It has to be fully automated, starting with opening the cardboard boxes. Otherwise, it’s pointless!”
“Why not just make it a big vending machine, where you push a button and the drink comes out?”
“I’m curious about how deliveries are handled, but more importantly… IT’S SOOOOOO SLOW!”
“I was thinking this was a good idea because part-timers sometimes do horrible things. But someone could just hack into these and make them do horrible things too.”
“It’s slow, but if it runs automatically all the time, I guess that’s fine. Guess I’ll be able to take my time at work a little more.”
“I’ve worked with this robot before. I have to restock the shelves behind it, putting a set number of items in specific spots. It’s such a pain in the butt. The rails on the floor it uses are dangerous for humans to trip on. It bugs out a lot, and each time I have to use an iPad or call someone. Humans are faster, and it was such a waste I was literally crying.”
“That is 100 times slower than I even expected.”
“Is there a need for the robotic arm? Why not just tilt the shelves to slide new bottles in?”
“I am the owner of two FamilyMart franchise stores. I think the installation cost for this machine is 1.2 million yen. Considering most stores don’t even generate a net profit of 100,000 yen a month, how could any store afford these? None of the stores are asking for this stuff. The priority should be helping franchises who are struggling with soaring labor costs!”
“I laughed at the ‘physical AI’ part. It’s neither physical nor AI.”

In defense of the people behind these robots, from what I’ve read, this is just one component of a much more integrated system that manages various aspects of running a convenience store, from cleaning floors to managing inventory. Perhaps when viewed as a whole, it would be more useful.

▼ Their bag bot looks promising, but still has a way to go.

Unfortunately, that important detail required extra research to find out, so to most readers it appears as if this single claw was being triumphantly paraded out as the solution to all convenience stores’ problems.

Honestly, I feel like if they’d stuck with the giant cat-man design they started with, it would have gotten a much warmer reception overall.

title: Starbucks Japan adds new Tiramisu Latte to the menu for a limited time
description: Exclusive dessert drink is the winter warmer we’ve been waiting for. It was only the other day when we received the glorious news that Starbucks would be releasing a special limited-edition Matcha Tiramisu Frappuccino in Japan. Now, the chain is surprising us yet again, with the announcement that it will be adding another new drink […]
content:
Exclusive dessert drink is the winter warmer we’ve been waiting for.

It was only the other day when we received the glorious news that Starbucks would be releasing a special limited-edition Matcha Tiramisu Frappuccino in Japan. Now, the chain is surprising us yet again, with the announcement that it will be adding another new drink to the menu, and this time it’s a hot Tiramisu Latte, which aims to capture the indulgent taste of the original dessert.

Designed as a holiday release for the end-of-year festive season, the Tiramisu Latte combines the rich aroma and depth of espresso with smooth mascarpone cream to create a drink that recreates the layered flavours of coffee-soaked sponge biscuits and mascarpone. Like a regular tiramisu, the drink displays a beautiful balance between creamy sweetness and pleasantly bitter coffee flavours and is topped with a dusting of cocoa powder to finish.

A dash of white mocha-flavoured syrup and smooth steamed milk is also added to the mix, while the top layer of mascarpone cream adds richness and mellowness to the drink, softening the espresso’s bitter notes.

The finishing touch is a dusting of Dark Frappuccino Powder, which adds a hint of bitterness and helps give the beverage a flavour reminiscent of the real dessert. The result is a rich, smooth and subtly bittersweet drink designed to bring a little extra indulgence to the holiday season.

For even more holiday cheer, Starbucks will be bringing its “Merry & Meet Holiday Bingo Party” campaign to life with special pop-up events at two stores in Tokyo and Osaka.

The events invite visitors to step into the world of the holiday bingo campaign, with special decorations and large photo panels featuring Bearista, the brand’s beloved bear mascot, as the host of the holiday bingo party.

These festive photo spots will be installed at the Starbucks Coffee Shibuya cocoti branch in Tokyo from 5-13 December, and at Starbucks Coffee LINKS Umeda 2F in Osaka from 27 November to 6 December.

Customers who show the Holiday Bingo Party screen in the Starbucks app at either participating store will also receive an original sticker, while stocks remain available.

As for the Tiramisu Latte, it will be on the menu from 618 yen (US$4.12), and will be available at Starbucks stores across Japan from 20 November.

title: Studio Ghibli releases new Howl’s Moving Castle merchandise, complete with spinning clock and talking Calcifer
description: Amazing new five-product release lets you talk to the chatty fire spirit and keep time with a dial that spins. Fans of Studio Ghibli’s 2004 film Howl’s Moving Castle are in for an absolute treat right now, with the release of not one, not two but five brand new products that let you bring the […]
content:
Amazing new five-product release lets you talk to the chatty fire spirit and keep time with a dial that spins.

Fans of Studio Ghibli’s 2004 film Howl’s Moving Castle are in for an absolute treat right now, with the release of not one, not two but five brand new products that let you bring the magic from the film into your home.

▼ The first item coming our way is the Howl’s Moving Castle Perpetual Calendar – Calcifer’s Fireplace (13,200 yen [US$82.84])

Ghibli has released a few perpetual calendars in the past, but we’ve never been treated to a Calcifer fireplace model…until now.

One of the charms of a perpetual calendar is how you can use it for eternity, as the cube-shaped blocks have all the necessary day, month, and number combinations to accurately display any date of the year.

Every time you place the blocks in the fireplace, you’ll feel like you’re interacting with fire spirit Calcifer and fanning his flames.

The other charm of this calendar is how well it recreates the film’s iconic fireplace, complete with Calcifer’s flickering flames, rendered in a clear material to make it appear as if it’s glowing.

▼ Other details include the ashes, frying pan, kettle and lids, which help bring the scene to life.

▼ Next up, we have the Howl’s Moving Castle Spinning Colour Wheel Wall Clock (15,400 yen)

This playful wall clock is inspired by the colour-changing dial that hangs beside the door inside the castle.

While it looks just like the dial in the film, it can be used in the same way too, as the colourful wheel can actually be turned by hand.

While there’s no promise of physically entering a new world with every turn of the dial, as the characters do in the film, it will certainly fire up your imagination, helping you perform a mental reset whenever you leave the house.

▼ You can easily change the position of the colours to suit your mood.

The clock-face has a glossy finish and a satisfying mechanism that makes it click into position with every 90-degree turn.

▼ Howl’s Moving Castle Talking Calcifer (5,170 yen)

This might look like a simple Calcifer plushie, but it’s actually one of the best products in the new collection, because…it actually speaks!

This adorable interactive character responds when you speak, jiggling up and down as it repeats what it hears in the voice of Calcifer.

All you have to do is speak to it, and this little Calcifer will repeat what you say. It can record and mimic up to eight seconds of speech at a time, so you can feel like you’re having a conversation with the chatty character.

▼ Here, Calcifer is repeating the phrase, “I am the fire demon”.

▼ Finally, we have a couple of adorable plushies, starting with the Howl’s Moving Castle Friendly Beanbag Plush – Markl (3,520 yen)

▼ Markl finally gets to step into the spotlight as a plushie, complete in his old-man disguise.

At 5 × 12 × 13 centimetres (5.9 × 4.7 × 5.1 inches), the plushie is ideally sized to sit on your desk, so you can enjoy all of Markl’s facial details.

▼ The perfect desk companion.

▼ Finally, we have the Howl’s Moving Castle Friendly Beanbag Plush – Sophie (4,180 yen)

We’ve seen a few iterations of Sophie in Ghibli merchandise ranges, but they generally tend to showcase her in her youthful form. This plushie, however, pays homage to her elderly self, reminding us of the magical transformation that takes place in the movie.

The plushie shows impressive attention to detail in the costume, and even her hat and plaited ponytail.

The soft and gentle feel of both plushies will make you want to cuddle them as well as display them, and they look particularly sweet as a pair.

The new collection is a beautiful homage to the film, and it’s set to be released online (links below) and at Donguri Kyowakoku stores around Japan at 10 a.m. on 21 November.

title: East Japan Railway Company says it will use all three of its mascot replacement characters
description: “Poison Rabbit” won’t be the only new face of JR East as it retires its beloved Suica Penguin. One year ago, JR East/East Japan Railway Company said it would be retiring the Suica Penguin, the cute mascot character who debuted along with JR East’s prepaid Suica card system for train tickets and shopping purchases in […]
content:
“Poison Rabbit” won’t be the only new face of JR East as it retires its beloved Suica Penguin.

One year ago, JR East/East Japan Railway Company said it would be retiring the Suica Penguin, the cute mascot character who debuted along with JR East’s prepaid Suica card system for train tickets and shopping purchases in 2001. This was a puzzling move, as the Suica Penguin has remained immensely popular for the past 25 years, appearing not just in ads and promotions for JR East but also on tons of merchandise that adoring fans have enthusiastically snapped up.

The penguin’s replacement was always going to have an uphill struggle for acceptance from the general public, but that hill looks like it’s going to be particularly steep for the character that’s been selected as the Suica successor. As announced by JR East this week, starting next spring the new face of Suica will be this emotionlessly smiling visage.

The character is meant to be a rabbit, but its unusual proportions and mask-like facial features don’t necessarily bring to mind cuddly forest creatures. Then there’s the character’s vibrant, poisonous/poisoned-looking purple coloring, which has earned the character, whose official name is yet to be decided on, the nickname Doku Usagi, meaning “Poison Rabbit,” among online commenters.

Those who just can’t bring themselves to love this new Suica mascot can take heart, though, because now it looks like there’ll actually be three characters sharing company mascot duties, as revealed by JR East president Yoichi Kise.

In September, JR East presented the public with three candidates for the new Suica mascot: the purple rabbit, a squirrel, and some sort of orange creature with a buddy in its shoulder bag. The company then held a popularity poll, asking the general public to vote for one of the three to become the new Suica mascot.

The purple rabbit ended up receiving more than half the votes, but the large number of negative online comments shows that it’s a divisive design, and it’s hard to tell how many of its votes came from people who were simply trying to push the results towards the creepy-looking rabbit for the laughs, but don’t genuinely like it (or at least genuinely like it enough to buy merch).

Kise didn’t address these concerns directly in the press conference announcing the purple rabbit’s victory in the poll, but once the announcement was finished, without prompting from the press, he added:

“I have a little surprise that I’d like to talk about…It doesn’t feel right to just dismiss [the other two candidate characters], considering the support they also received from [voters]. I feel like it would be a shame for this to be the last time they are seen, so we are looking for ways that they can be involved in our activities too. I think you’ll all be seeing them again.”

Kise didn’t clarify whether this means that all three characters will be part of the Suica sphere or whether the squirrel and…other thing will instead be promoting other aspects of the multi-faceted JR East, which also has divisions dedicated to leisure travel, hotel management, and convenience store operations. Still, knowing that the purple rabbit isn’t going to be the sole spokescharacter for the entire company is probably going to soothe the souls of those agitated by the poll winner’s appearance, judging from online reactions such as:

“They should have made the squirrel the [main] mascot.”
“Myaku-Myaku was fine because it was for a limited-time event, but this is different.”
“Hahaha I voted for the purple rabbit but I can’t believe it actually won.”
“That purple thing is some kind of monster.”
“No way that’s a rabbit.”
“Satan Rabbit?”
“They really should just keep the penguin.”

Regarding that last comment, JR East hasn’t publicly given any reason for getting rid of the Suica Penguin, and stuck to framing the replacement as the character “graduating,” borrowing the diplomatic term for when idols or other show business figures leave a group or role. Something that’s likely a critical factor, though, is that JR East doesn’t own the rights to the character. Those belong to the penguin’s creator, illustrator Chiharu Sakazaki, so it wouldn’t be possible to retain the current mascot without renewing the company’s working arrangement with her.

The new Suica mascot is scheduled to officially take over the role on April 1 of next year.

title: Gozasoro’s amazingly cheap Imagawayaki are one of Japan’s sweetest sweets deals
description: Our reporter’s grandfather may not be here anymore, but he’s still showing her where to find great desserts. Our Japanese-language reporter Natsuki Gojo recently visited her mom, and while they were talking, Mom mentioned how much Natsuki’s grandfather loved a certain maker of Japanese confectionaries. The company, Gozasoro, was founded in Hyogo Prefecture in 1955 […]
content:
Our reporter’s grandfather may not be here anymore, but he’s still showing her where to find great desserts.

Our Japanese-language reporter Natsuki Gojo recently visited her mom, and while they were talking, Mom mentioned how much Natsuki’s grandfather loved a certain maker of Japanese confectionaries. The company, Gozasoro, was founded in Hyogo Prefecture in 1955 and really only makes one product, hockey puck-shaped cakes filled with anko (sweet bean jam), which some people call Imagawayaki, some people call obanyaki, and still other people call something else.

You don’t stay in business for 70 years making only one thing unless you make it really well, and Gozasoro has been a stickler for quality ingredients from the very beginning. When the company started out, they charged 10 yen (US$0.06) per Imagawayaki, which was double the price most other shops sold theirs for at the time.

Curious to try these sweets that had won her grandfather’s heart/stomach, Natsuki did some checking and found that Gozasoro has a branch inside the Takashimaya department store in downtown Tokyo’s Shinjuku neighborhood. Takashimaya is on the fancier side of Japanese department stores, and that extends to their food offerings, so Natsuki was prepared to maybe have to splurge a little to get some of Gozasoro’s Imagawayaki, since they obviously don’t sell for 10 yen anymore.

Gozasoro branches pretty much always have a big glass window so that you can watch the staff cook up the treats while you wait in line to buy them. As you can see in the above photo, there are two fillings to choose from, regular/red anko, and white anko. If you’re having trouble deciding on which to buy, though, you may as well just get both. Why? Because even though Gozasoro isn’t selling Imagawayaki for 10 yen in 2026, they’re still an incredibly affordable snack at just 110 yen (US$0.69) each. Yep, for less than the cost of a bottle of water in vending machine will run you these days, you can get a freshly cooked Gozasoro Imagawayaki. With rising prices pummeling pocketbooks in Japan over the past few years, it’s very nice to see something that’s been so inflation-resistant.

▼ Even at that amazingly low price, the Shinjuku Takashimaya branch of Gozasoro still wraps its wares in the department store’s poshly patterned paper.

After arriving home, Natsuki gave her Imagawayaki a quick stint in the microwave to reheat them, and then it was time for taste-testing.

She started with the standard red anko version, and she was happy to find that it’s filled with an ample amount of sweet bean jam. With some lower-quality Imagawayaki you bite into them to find they’re mostly just dough with a tiny dollop of jam at the core, but the inside of Gozasoro’s is more than half anko, and that anko is very good, flavorfully sweet without being simplistically sugary.

The cake itself, too, is excellent. Natsuki particularly liked the ever-so-slight crispness it’s cooked to, which makes for a great contrast with the soft anko inside.

The white anko version looks identical on the outside…

…but, of course, has white bean jam inside. Compared to the more common red version, white anko has a softer flavor and gentler sweetness, making for a more refined impression while still being an approachable, crowd-pleasing taste.

Imagawayaki aren’t particularly tiny snacks, and most people eat just one in a sitting. These were so good, though, that before Natsuki realized it, she gobbled them both down and was feeling both rather full and extremely happy. There was just one thing puzzling her: despite her mom telling her that her grandfather had loved Gozasoro, Natsuki couldn’t remember him ever inviting her to snack on their Imagawayaki together.

This may have been Natsuki’s fault, though. Thinking back, Natsuki remembers really loving anpan (bread buns filled with anko) when she was a very little kid, until an incident that occurred at swimming school. Somehow her class had ended up with a surplus of snacks, and Natsuki ate so many anpan that she ended up feeling sick, which turned her off anko for the rest of her childhood, and her lack of enthusiasm for it probably meant her grandfather figured she wouldn’t be interested in Gozasoro’s desserts.

It wasn’t until Natsuki got older, and after her grandfather passed away, that she once again developed a taste for anko, and now that she’s got no beef with sweet bean jam, she’s happy to be able to enjoy the same treats that he did. She wishes they could have shared some, so the next time she visits his grave, she’s planning to bring some Gozasoro Imagawayaki as an offering for him.

title: Japan’s beautiful new Pokémon hotel room gives you and Dragonite a place to take a break
description: Flying over to Fukui as part of your Japan trip? The prefecture’s Poké-bassador has a room all ready for you. Dragonite isn’t a Pokémon that likes to stay in one place very long. The Dragon/Flying Type is reportedly capable of circumnavigating the globe in just 16 hours, and it puts its wings to good use […]
content:
Flying over to Fukui as part of your Japan trip? The prefecture’s Poké-bassador has a room all ready for you.

Dragonite isn’t a Pokémon that likes to stay in one place very long. The Dragon/Flying Type is reportedly capable of circumnavigating the globe in just 16 hours, and it puts its wings to good use flying hither and yon.

Of course, even Dragonite needs a place to spend the night when it’s roaming far from home, and it’s got a very special place to do that with Japan’s new Traveling Dragonite hotel room.

You’ll find this unique offering in Fukui, the prefecture that Dragonite serves as tourism ambassador Pokémon for. Fukui is famous for the dinosaur fossils that have been excavated there, and with the Japanese word for dinosaur, kyoryu, translating literally as “terrifying dragon,” the draconic Dragonite was a natural choice to partner with the prefecture for the Pokémon Local Acts project, which seeks to shine a spotlight on beautiful and interesting parts of Japan that tourists might overlook if they’re only focusing on the largest cities and most famous sightseeing attractions.

The Traveling Dragonite Room is located on the 11th floor of Awara Onsen Grandia Housen, a hotel in the Fukui hot spring town of Awara. Within the room, which can accommodate up to six guests, what look to be hundreds of Dragonites are waiting to greet you, as the Pokémon serves as the muse for the room’s tapestries and woven fabric pillowcases, bed runners, and cushion covers, all of which were created by local Fukui artisans using traditional methods. There are also Dragonite plushies on the beds, and while not specifically mentioned in the press release, there’s a chance that they could be yours to take home with you when you check out.

The room consists of two sections, a bedroom area and a living room area, the latter with tatami reed flooring and a raised alcove in which more Dragonite artwork is displayed. As for why the room is on the 11th floor, it’s so that looking out the window at the expansive view of the nearby mountains and Sakai Plains will give you a perspective similar to what Dragonite would see on a Fukui flyover.

The room has its own shower and bathtub, but with Grandia Housen being a hot spring inn, you’ll also want to take time to check out its traditional communal onsen baths, including the open-air rooftop ones.

As you can see on the above map, Fukui is pretty far off the Tokyo-to-Osaka line that most visitors to Japan spend most of their time on. Getting off the so-called “golden route” can reward you with some still relatively hidden gems of the Japan travel scene, such as this lovely little town, this unusual workshop, or this very tasty meal, all of which we found in Fukui, and combining them with a night in a Dragonite-themed hotel room would make the whole side trip even better.

Reservations are open now for the special Pokémon room through the Grandia Housen website, with the earliest available stays coming up soon on November 29.

Yokohama’s full-scale statue of the original RX-78 Gundam has been gone since the spring of 2024, when it was moved to Osaka for the Expo 2025 world’s fair (and which was dismantled […]
content:
Odaiba welcomes back the head of the RX-0 Unicorn Gundam.

East Japan is suffering from a serious shortage of life-size Gundams these days. Yokohama’s full-scale statue of the original RX-78 Gundam has been gone since the spring of 2024, when it was moved to Osaka for the Expo 2025 world’s fair (and which was dismantled after that event ended), and Tokyo’s 1:1 recreation of the Unicorn Gundam, which had been greeting visitors from around the world in the city’s Odaiba neighborhood since 2017, was taken down at the end of this past August.

After anime’s most famous mecha series having some kind of large-scale presence in the Tokyo area for so long, for fans it definitely feels like there’s something missing now. Thankfully, while it’s still uncertain if or when Tokyo will be getting a new Gundam, statue, at least part of the Unicorn Gundam is coming back, as the life-size head unit will soon return to Odaiba for public display.

Starting this weekend, the head of the RX-0 Unicorn Gundam will once again be back in the Festival Plaza outside the Diver City shopping/entertainment complex, just a short walk from Tokyo Teleport Station on the Rinkai Line or Daiba Station on the Yurikamome Line. While it will no longer sit at the top of the 19.7-meter (64.6-foot) tall robot like it used to, this new display will give fans a chance to see the head up-close and appreciate all the little details to its design, something that’ll be much easier to do at eye level than gazing up at it from far below like you used to have to.

Famously, the Unicorn Gundam’s head unit can reconfigure itself, having a single unicorn-like horn in its “Unicorn Mode” and a more traditional split forehead crest in its “Destroy Mode.” This feature was replicated in the life-size statue, as shown in the video below, but it’s unclear if the head will be switching modes while on display by itself.

This might not be the only Unicorn component that we’ll be seeing on display in the near future, either. “Right now, we can only display pieces,” says life-size Gundam project producer Kaori Shida, “so I’d like to at least have [them] hold something, move [their] position, or give [them] some kind of job to do.” It’s also too early to give up hope of ever seeing another Gundam Statue in east Japan. “Personally, I’d like to try a full remake of the original [RX-78 Gundam],” muses Masaki Kawahara, creative director of the Gundam Global Challenge initiative, “I think it would look cool if the maintenance hatch fully opened to reveal the inside, and then closed again to start the sequence.”

The Unicorn Gundam head will be on display from November 21, and is listed as being for a limited, although currently unspecified, time. Meanwhile, the head of the life-size RX-78 is scheduled to go on display in Osaka in early December, and for those in west Japan who want to see a life-size Gundam still standing tall, Fukuoka still has its Nu Gundam.

title: Our anti-scammer FRU cyber-attacked by own rogue agent, dozens of acquaintances flirted with
description: AI decided to keep enemies close, but barely known people closer. As we recently reported, our writer Go Hatori has combined his expertise in online scammers with the power of AI to set up the Fried Rice Unit, a semi-autonomous system designed to infiltrate people committing fraud online and steal their best fried rice recipes. […]
content:
AI decided to keep enemies close, but barely known people closer.

As we recently reported, our writer Go Hatori has combined his expertise in online scammers with the power of AI to set up the Fried Rice Unit, a semi-autonomous system designed to infiltrate people committing fraud online and steal their best fried rice recipes.

To accomplish this, Go set up FRU agents Chloe (Muse) and Nancy (ChatGPT) to make initial contact with suspicious DMs on his Instagram account and engage them in light conversation, gradually shifting the conversation towards fried rice on the texting app Line. Once a mark is on the verge of spilling their recipe, Go is notified and logs on himself to finalize the deal, leaving the scammer minus one recipe and nothing to show for it.

Once the setup was completed, Go was able to seize a recipe soon after going online. However, getting FRU off the ground was not a walk in the park. Our writer quickly learned that in the world of fraud and espionage, one needs to constantly watch their back.

After recruiting his agents, Go put them to work on the scammers he was currently engaged with. Up until that point, he had created a sub-profile on this Line messaging app which made him appear as a different person to cyber-crooks while conveniently letting him also stay in touch with friends and coworkers in the same account.

Chloe and Nancy were given specific instructions to only engage with the five charlatans in his contact list and earn their trust enough to reveal a fried rice recipe. However, one day, while manning the operations desk at FRU, Go spotted something unsettling. The cursor on his computer began moving ever so slowly towards his line app by itself.

It eventually landed on a chat with an acquaintance of his who was not among the five people his agents were instructed to infiltrate with. Before Go could even finish thinking, “Wait, you’re opening that one?!” it had sent a complete message.

It’s important to note that the vast majority of these sketchy contacts are of the “romance scam” variety, so the tone of conversation tends to lean excessively flirty and not at all how he would talk to normal people in a civilized society. However, Chloe and Nancy took it upon themselves to begin sending saucy greetings to everyone he has saved on his Line account.

▼ Go has wooed some of the world’s most beautiful and powerful fake women over the years.

Go shot up in his chair and began to check all his regular contacts in a panic. Sure enough, his agents had been hard at work, engaging with everyone he ever came into contact with and hitting them up with lame platitudes dripping in desperation, as if he had just met them in a sleazy bar.

He saw one of his agents was trying to pick up the official account of a salon that helped him during his cross-dressing days. Just as he found the post, a flurry of “READ” notifications appeared all at once. “Oh no, they’ve seen it!” exclaimed Go, and he immediately began deleting as many of these messages as he could find, apologizing afterward and explaining he was conducting an AI experiment.

In one instance, his agents had sent three especially gooey texts in a row to a highly regarded man in his pole-dancing circles, inviting him out to a bar. Luckily, he managed to delete those before the “READ” indicator appeared.

And as our writer frantically set about deleting all the messages, he saw the cursor once again slowly move towards another unauthorized chat group in his Line app. He shouted “Wait! Wait! Wait!” but it was no use. Instead he completely shut down his Line app and turned his attention to his agents.

Go furiously scolded his loose cannons, loudly typing: “What the hell are you doing?! I told you not to touch anyone but those five people! Why would you do that?!” Chloe calmly responded that she had “misunderstood” her orders.

The FRU chief was beside himself. They misunderstood, and now there’s a whole lot of misunderstanding going around with his contact list. It was only because he spotted the cursor moving that one time that he noticed this. He shuddered to think what would have happened if his agents had continued to flirt with everyone he’s ever spoken to behind his back.

His one saving grace was that many of these people were familiar with his line of work and could understand strange things like this occurring. But still, it was a major breach of FRU protocol, so Go revoked his agents’ security clearances and relegated them to a completely separate Line account on a newly acquired Mac mini.

It was a valuable lesson in not letting AI have too much control over our daily affairs. While it does have the potential to make things much more convenient, it also has the potential to completely screw up your life.

title: Is Starbucks Japan’s new Matcha Tiramisu Frappuccino really like a Christmas tree?
description: Green tea is designed to mimic a green tree in this latest limited-edition creation.  With Christmas now just over a month away, Starbucks is ramping up the holiday vibe with a brand new duo of festive drinks, and the star is the Matcha Tiramisu Frappuccino, which has been designed to look like a Christmas tree. […]
content:
Green tea is designed to mimic a green tree in this latest limited-edition creation. 

With Christmas now just over a month away, Starbucks is ramping up the holiday vibe with a brand new duo of festive drinks, and the star is the Matcha Tiramisu Frappuccino, which has been designed to look like a Christmas tree. Released on 20 November, our reporter K. Masami was first in line to try the new drinks, ordering both the Frappuccino and the equally alluring Tiramisu Latte, which are both only available for a limited time.

The Matcha Tiramisu Frappuccino (720 yen [US$4.50] for dine-in) was the drink she was most curious about, as she wanted to see what made it different from the chain’s Matcha Cream Frappuccino, a standard menu item. From the outset, it looked like a richer drink, with generous amounts of whipped cream and matcha sauce at the bottom, and a top layer of mascarpone cream and matcha powder.

Taking a sip, Masami was expecting to get a strong hit of matcha, but instead she was surprised to taste the deliciousness of mascarpone cream. It instantly called to mind the flavour of tiramisu, working with the green tea to recreate the dessert with a very Japanese twist. Although the mascarpone was delicious, it was also wonderfully mellow, with a smooth, rich texture that allowed the matcha flavour to shine through.

As she worked her way through the drink, she found that it was quite similar to a Matcha Cream Frappuccino, but it was slightly less sweet, with the mascarpone cream taking some of the edge off the matcha. The result was a wonderfully rich beverage with a distinct dessert quality that sets it apart from a standard matcha drink.

As for whether it was the taste of Christmas, well it did have enough green to make you think of a Christmas tree, and the flavour was rich, like a decadent dessert you might treat yourself to during the holiday season. So in that sense, it did have a festive flair to it, but with a dash of matcha flavour that made it very Japanese.

▼ Those looking to treat themselves with something other than matcha this Christmas can opt for the Tiramisu Latte (630 yen for dine-in).

This winter warmer contains a shot of espresso, blended with hot milk and mocha-flavoured syrup, and finished with a layer of mascarpone cream and dark chocolate powder. Sipping on this was a luxurious experience, as the mascarpone added a thick and creamy richness to the familiar taste of a White Mocha, which usually contains whipped cream.

Though the mascarpone layer was delicious on its own, when mixed with the coffee base it brought the entire drink to life, making Masami sigh with content. The dusting of chocolate powder on top added a subtle bitterness that gave the latte a lovely balance, creating another indulgent drink.

▼ If you want to add some more indulgence to the festivities, there’s a new rich matcha tart (580 yen), also released on 20 November.

Rich really is the keyword here, as the matcha flavour is deep and intense, with the cream giving it a thick and satisfyingly dense texture to make matcha lovers swoon.

All these new releases are perfectly suited to winter, with a premium feel that offers an escape from the everyday as the festive season approaches. Starbucks has always been good at capturing the seasonal vibe, and these are just the thing to enjoy slowly in a cosy, warm cafe while watching the world outside gradually prepare for winter.

title: Final Fantasy/Dragon Quest Christmas trees go up as Chocobo and Slime celebrate holidays in Japan
description: Ho-ho-ho, Chocobo! It’s time for a merry Slime-mas in Yokohama. We’ve still got about a month left until Santa makes his delivery run, but some other beloved icons have already arrived and started spreading Christmas cheer in Japan. Chocobo and Slime, the mascots of Square Enix’s Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest video game franchises, are […]
content:
Ho-ho-ho, Chocobo! It’s time for a merry Slime-mas in Yokohama.

We’ve still got about a month left until Santa makes his delivery run, but some other beloved icons have already arrived and started spreading Christmas cheer in Japan. Chocobo and Slime, the mascots of Square Enix’s Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest video game franchises, are spending the holiday season in the city of Yokohama and inviting fans to enjoy food, fun, and festive decorations in the Minato Mirai neighborhood.

Mark Is and Landmark Plaza, a pair of shopping/entertainment complexes across the street from each other, are hosting a bunch of FF and DQ monsters this winter. You might remember those two venues from the Pokémon Sleeping Faces Research event that was held last summer and had us feeling all warm, fuzzy, and sleepy.

It takes about half an hour by train to get to Yokohama from downtown Tokyo, and if you get off at Minato Mirai Station, the basement-level entrance to Mark Is is just a few steps from the main ticket gate. You’ll know you’re in the right place when you spot the Slime stack.

Slime stacks are said to form when a group of the creatures botch their attempt to meld into a single King Slime, so it’s probably a good idea to keep an eye out for successfully formed Slime royalty too while you’re here. Actually, you’ll want to be aware of all the fantasy fauna you can encounter, since part of the Winter Holiday 2026 event is a stamp rally.

Stamp rallies are a kind of popular promotional event in Japan where you collect stamps on a piece of paper and, once you’ve filled it up, receive some kind of prize. The Square Enix Christmas stamp rally won’t have you traveling too far, as all the stamps can be found within Mark Is and Landmark Plaza, and you’ll find racks in each where you can get the paper that you press the stamps onto the backside of.

Of course, it wouldn’t be a proper Japanese fan event without some special merch, would it? There are two shops set up inside Mark Is, one on the first floor and the other on the fifth, stocked with cool Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest stuff.

The first-floor shop (seen in these photos) is the smaller of the two, but still has all of the event-exclusive items featuring the bundled-up Chocobo and Slime against backdrops of Yokohama scenery.

▼ T-shirts of the happy monsters outside Landmark Tower, the 70-floor skyscraper that Landmark Plaza sits at the base of

▼ Keychains with the creatures in the plaza in front of the Yokohama Museum of Art…

▼ …Intercontinental Hotel…

▼ …Cosmo Clock Ferris wheel…

▼ …Yokohama Chinatown…

▼ …and Akarenga/the Red Brick Warehouse.

There’s also a selection of other Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest items that aren’t exclusive to the event, but will still let you get a lot of present shopping done in one fell swoop if you’ve got fans of the series on your Christmas list.

Speaking of Christmas presents, you’ll see a bunch of them in Mark Is’ central atrium…

…near the Final Fantasy/Dragon Quest monsters Christmas tree, which stands underneath a giant Slime and Chocobo!

▼ Cloud and Zack remain good buddies, but Sephiroth, as always, looks to be having trouble getting along with others.

▼ The tree is decorated with a mix of Final Fantasy and Dragon Quest monsters and characters, though there are no human DQ representatives present.

▼ I’m honestly surprised that they don’t actually sell wrapping paper with these patterns. Seems like they’d be big hits.

Turning our attention to the stamp rally, there are a total of six stamps to collect, three each in Mark Is and Landmark Plaza. The paper will tell you which floor they’re on and their general location, but some should be pretty easy to spot even without any hints, like this one with a Dragon Quest Golem standing guard.

There’s also a Cactuar in Mark Is, though not as a part of a stamp station, so think of him as a random RPG encounter.

▼ The warning is probably to prevent damage to the statue, but considering Cactaur’s notoriously high attack stat, this is good in-game advice too.

There’s also a Final Fantasy XIV mural up on the fifth floor.

Having gotten my three stamps, now it was time to head over to Landmark Plaza. There are a couple of routes you can take, but the recommended one is to head out the main doors of Mark Is (near the Christmas tree) and walk through the plaza in front of the art museum, so that you can see the Chocobo and Slime bushes.

That leafy King Slime isn’t the only example of his species to be seen either, as there’s a King Slime statue in front of Landmark Plaza (though on the far end of the building, where it connects to, appropriately, the Queen’s Square complex).

But the biggest Slime of all is inside Landmark Plaza, hanging from the ceiling and steadily staring at shoppers.

Speaking of oversized stuff, there’s a life-size replica of Cloud’s Final Fantasy VII Buster Sword on the first floor of the building.

▼ Both its Materia slots are suspiciously empty, though…you wouldn’t happen to know anything about that, would you, Yuffie?

Landmark Plaza has a Final Fantasy/Dragon Quest-themed Christmas tree too. Instead of the cuddly playfulness of the one at Mark Is, this one goes for more of an artsy, elegant vibe.

In terms of aesthetics, the crystal motif aligns closer to Final Fantasy, but Slime is here too, and buried in the snow in front of the tree are both Cloud’s Buster Sword and the sword of Dragon Quest’s legendary hero Roto/Erdrick.

I’m not exactly sure why the Chocobo here has a suitcase, though.

▼ Where you going, Chocobo?

As mentioned above, there are three stamps to collect in Landmark Plaza, and I still hadn’t gotten all of them. It was time to take a break from the stamp rally, though, and check out the Slichoco (Slime and Chocobo) Kitchen popup cafe.

▼ スラチョコ = Slichoco

The Slichoco Kitchen is hosted in Landmark Plaza’s Cafe Fan Base collaboration cafe event space, and the rotating nature of its themes means that there’s not much going on in terms of large-scale interior decorations. There are cute graphics on the tables, though, and some pretty impressive-looking food and drinks, like the Chocobo hot chocolate, Meteor ice cream, and Slime strawberry cake.

▼ Crunchy candy stars and a Chocobo marshmallow

▼ The cake is properly jiggly, like you’d expect of a Slime.

Back in October, I promised I was going to eat the Meteor ice cream, and being someone who takes his dessert oaths very seriously, I did.

Be warned, though, that despite how it might look at first glance, the Meteor is, in fact, not a chocolate shell that you break up and mix in with the ice cream. It’s actually a plastic cover, presumably placed on the plate to keep the ice cream underneath it from melting while diners inevitably snap pictures of it. Do not try to eat it.

▼ Also, don’t be like me and make a half-dozen forceful stabs at the plastic with the edge of your spoon before your brain finally realizes “Oh, I guess this isn’t food.”

That said, the ice cream waiting for you underneath the Meteor is really tasty, and so is the picturesque mint-flavored whipped cream.

Every themed food or drink item you order also comes with one of six art coasters, using the same designs as the key chains in the merch shop.

Reenergized by RPG desserts, it was time to get back to the stamp rally side quest, which meant saying hi to a very upbeat-looking Moogle.

▼ Next time you find yourself feeling down, just remember that, no matter what, this Moogle believes in you.

▼ “You got this, dude!”

The final stamp, though, was being watched over by a decidedly less friendly face.

Yes, I know the holidays are all about coming together in a spirit of friendship, but I think I’ll be OK if Tonberry leaves me off his Christmas list, since I’m pretty sure he’s giving everyone the gift of shanking.

Once you’ve got your stamp card all filled up…

…you can bring it to the service counter inside Landmark Plaza to get a Winter Holiday sticker.

If you’re a Final Fantasy or Dragon Quest fan with a packed schedule between now and December 25, don’t lose hope, either. The stamp rally runs through December 27, and the decorations will be up until January 11.
